flashcard_questions.q: What does the windmill represent in Soviet history?
Which ironic simile describes the animals' labour on the windmill?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘all that year the animals worked like slaves’

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the phrase ‘worked like slaves’ so ironic in this novel?
flashcard_questions.a: The whole purpose of the Rebellion was to free the animals from slavery.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Squealer explain Napoleon taking over the windmill plan?
flashcard_questions.a: He claims Napoleon only pretended to oppose it, to get rid of Snowball.

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation measures Boxer's strength against the other animals?
flashcard_questions.a: It was ‘equal to that of all the rest of the animals put together’.

flashcard_questions.q: Which image conveys Boxer's extreme physical effort at the windmill?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘the tips of his hoofs clawing at the ground’

flashcard_questions.q: Which second motto does Boxer adopt after Snowball's expulsion?
Which Soviet coal miner does Boxer parallel?
Which commandment do the pigs break by moving into the farmhouse?
flashcard_questions.a: The Fourth: ‘No animal shall sleep in a bed’.

flashcard_questions.q: What words are quietly added to the Fourth Commandment?
Which justification does Squealer give for the pigs' extra comforts?
flashcard_questions.a: They need comfort in order to do their ‘brainwork’.

flashcard_questions.q: What detail shows Squealer's propaganda is backed by the threat of force?
flashcard_questions.a: He is always ‘attended by two or three dogs’.

flashcard_questions.q: Who does Napoleon hire to handle trade with neighbouring farms?
What euphemism does Squealer use for the trading arrangement?
flashcard_questions.a: It is ‘not of course for any commercial purpose’.

flashcard_questions.q: Who does Napoleon blame when the storm destroys the windmill?
flashcard_questions.a: Snowball, who supposedly acted ‘in sheer malignity’.

notes: 15 cards: 8 character or theme to quotation, 3 symbol or event to significance (the windmill, the irony of 'like slaves', the dogs behind Squealer), 2 context-to-relevance (Stakhanov, Whymper), 2 commandment-change cards. Dropped scapegoating, proletariat, totalitarian and dramatic irony as glossary definition cards — all four are demonstrated by the quotation cards in this deck, so a definition direction would interfere.
